1161.quote_or_event: “That which is within them, comes out; it cannot be concealed by concealment.”
1161.explanation: Guru Nanak observes that whatever truly fills a person inside will surface, however hard they try to hide it.
1161.tie_back: The Kural's heroine tries to hide her love-pain, but it wells up like spring water the more she draws on it; Guru Nanak likewise says what is within cannot be hidden by hiding.
1161.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1243, Raag Saarang, Sarang ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1161._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match: the principle fits, but Guru Nanak is speaking of a person's inner character (in context, greed and falsehood) coming to light, not of love that will not stay hidden.

1162.quote_or_event: “Let's hug Him close in our embrace, and not feel shy; let's bathe our minds in the dust of His feet.”
1162.explanation: Guru Arjan urges the devotee to hold the Beloved close without any bashfulness and to humble the mind at His feet.
1162.tie_back: The Kural's heroine cannot hide her pain yet is too ashamed to tell it to the one who caused it; Guru Arjan asks the soul to set exactly that shyness aside before the divine Beloved.
1162.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 846, Raag Bilaaval, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1162._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match by contrast: the Kural honours the heroine's modesty (naan) as a virtue, while Guru Arjan tells the devotee not to be shy before the Lord.

1163.quote_or_event: “Each and every hair on my head, and my mind and body, suffer the pains of separation; without seeing my God, I cannot sleep.”
1163.explanation: Guru Ram Das describes separation from God as a pain carried in every part of the body and mind.
1163.tie_back: The Kural pictures the heroine's worn body carrying love and shame like loads on a shoulder pole; Guru Ram Das likewise describes a body and mind wholly burdened by the pain of separation.
1163.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 836, Raag Bilaaval, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1163._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match: it shares the image of a body loaded with longing, but has nothing of the Kural's carrying-pole or its balance of love against shame.

1164.quote_or_event: “The terrifying world-ocean is difficult and dreadful; there is no shore on this side or the one beyond. There is no boat, no raft, no oars and no boatman.”
1164.explanation: Guru Nanak describes the world as a fearful ocean with no visible shore and no boat or raft to cross it, a crossing made possible only by the Guru.
1164.tie_back: The Kural's heroine says a sea of love lies before her but there is no safe raft to cross it; Guru Nanak uses the same image of a vast sea with no raft.
1164.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 59, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1164._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa, two consecutive lines); near one-to-one on the sea with no raft, though Guru Nanak's sea is worldly existence rather than love, and in Gurbani the Guru is the raft.

1165.quote_or_event: “O my Husband Lord, You are angry with me in Your Mind. The fault is with me, and not with my Husband Lord.”
1165.explanation: Sheikh Farid, speaking as the soul-bride, feels the Husband Lord's displeasure but lays the blame on her own failings, not on Him.
1165.tie_back: The Kural's heroine reproaches her husband, asking what he would do as an enemy if he brings such sorrow as a lover; Farid's bride feels the same estrangement but turns the reproach on herself.
1165.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 794, Raag Soohee, Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1165._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match by contrast: the Kural blames the beloved, while Gurbani teaches the soul-bride to blame her own faults, never the Lord.

1166.quote_or_event: “Emotional attachment to Maya is a treacherous ocean of pain and poison, which cannot be crossed.”
1166.explanation: Guru Amar Das calls attachment (moh) an ocean of pain so vast it cannot be crossed by one's own effort.
1166.tie_back: The Kural says love's joy is as wide as the sea but its sorrow is wider still; Guru Amar Das likewise measures the sorrow born of attachment as an uncrossable ocean.
1166.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1417, Salok Vaaran te Vadheek, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1166._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match only: it shares the ocean-of-sorrow image, but Gurbani treats the attachment behind this sorrow (moh, one of the five thieves) as a fault to overcome, whereas the Kural treats love itself as a worthy sea of joy.

1167.quote_or_event: “I cannot endure the night, and sleep does not come, without the Sight of the Beloved Guru's Court.”
1167.explanation: Guru Arjan writes of nights that will not end and sleep that will not come while he is parted from his Beloved Guru; Sikh tradition holds that these verses were sent as letters to his father, Guru Ram Das, while he was kept away in Lahore.
1167.tie_back: The Kural's heroine swims a flood of love that has no shore and lies alone awake through the midnight watch; Guru Arjan likewise describes the sleepless night of one parted from the beloved.
1167.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 97, Raag Maajh, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1167._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); good fit on the sleepless night of separation, but it lacks the flood-without-shore image, the longing is for the Guru, and the Lahore letters story is tradition, not checked here.

1168.quote_or_event: “Like a patient nearing his death, whom should I tell this state that has resulted due to the fire of separation? All these things (moon, stars, dresses etc.) are becoming uncomfortable and painful for me, whereas all these are highly peace-giving and source of comfort for the whole world.”
1168.explanation: Bhai Gurdas has the separated lover say that the moon, stars and other things that comfort everyone else only torment her. His Kabitt Savaiye are early exegesis, not scripture.
1168.tie_back: The Kural's heroine pities the night, which has lulled every creature to sleep and is left with her alone for company; Bhai Gurdas's lover likewise finds that what soothes the whole world leaves her alone in her pain.
1168.source: Bhai Gurdas, Kabitt Savaiye 668, English translation as given in the BaniDB database
1168._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (kabitt 668, closing line); good fit on being the lone sufferer while the world rests, though the night is not personified as a companion and the Beloved is the Lord.

1169.quote_or_event: “When I could not be with You for just one moment, the Dark Age of Kali Yuga dawned for me.”
1169.explanation: Guru Arjan says that even a moment apart from his Beloved Guru stretched into a whole dark age; Sikh tradition places this verse among his letters from Lahore.
1169.tie_back: The Kural's heroine finds the long nights of separation crueller even than the husband who left; Guru Arjan likewise describes how time apart from the beloved swells into an age of darkness.
1169.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 96, Raag Maajh, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1169._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); good fit on time made endless by separation, though it has no comparison of cruelties and the longing is for the Guru.

1170.quote_or_event: “Ascending to His Mansion, I gaze upon His path, and my eyes are filled with tears.”
1170.explanation: Guru Arjan pictures the waiting bride climbing to the roof to watch the road for her Husband, her eyes filling with tears.
1170.tie_back: The Kural's heroine wishes her eyes could go to her husband as her heart does, instead of swimming in a flood of tears; Guru Arjan's bride can only watch the road with tear-filled eyes while her heart goes out to the Beloved.
1170.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 624, Raag Sorath, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1170._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong fit on tearful eyes that cannot reach the absent beloved, though the Kural's contrast between heart and eyes is only implied, and the love is spiritual.
